Title: Let's Go Out Tonight
Comment: The name of the artist on this recording actually stays in my area in Glasgow-technically Paul Buchanan was never really Glaswegian .  I'm going to talk a little about Glasgow here -I lost one of my greatest friends on Easter Monday . Ironically Gordon was American but moved back to Glasgow in the late 60's-a story that was always told as being due to his parents splitting up. There's a sting in that tale. I will recount on the follow up replies. Me and Gordon met in 1982 when Glasgow was a thriving centre of cool-if that matters but him being 4 years older than me-he took me under his wing and we went to the best bars and clubs. Music was central to us-he wasn't a rock fan per se -and we gelled on The Blue Nile and I turned him onto Eitzel. We went to the football together for over 40 years and he looked after me when I really needed it and was an uniquely good person. I miss him deeply so this is for him. . I miss the Glasgow of this song too.

Title: Interpretes
Comment:
"I wanna go back to my home town
Though I know it'll never be the same"
- Joe Jackson

This is a timely round, as I am actually spending the summer with family in Midland, Michigan (USA). 

Years ago, I was home on break from university, and like many young folks I took a short-term job to make some extra money. I was part of a rotating work crew for our local public works department, doing various tasks like pouring sidewalks, filling potholes, and clearing brush.

One of my supervisors was a friendly man named Ivan. We were at lunch one day when he told a story about going to see his son play in a band opening for Neil Young. It took me a minute, but I figured out he was referring to Steve Shelley of Sonic Youth (who, by the way, is the spitting image of his father).

We've already had SY and current collaborator Bill Orcutt, so here's a track from Shelley's 2009 team-up with Chicago indie rock artists Disappears and White/Light, eventually released on Shelley's own label in 2020.

Title: Love Bird
Comment: Welcome to Snoqualmie, birthplace of Ella Raines (watch "Tall In the Saddle" with John Wayne if you ever get a chance).  Issaquah, the second town west on Interstate 90, would have given you Modest Mouse.  Instead, here's a 2017 offering from Snoqualmie local Strong Sun Moon (an acoustic world-fusion and roots group featuring Camelia Jade and Mike Antone).  The alternate choice was Mother Root, a heavy sludge/doom duo.  You're welcome.

Title: New York, Let's Do Nothing
Comment: I felt sure we’d had King Hannah before, but the spreadsheet says no. My favourite Liverpool band of recent years, an irresistible mix of Mazzy Star, Neil Young and PJ Harvey, with a fondness for chatty but surreal lyrics - shining stars in a city currently with an apparently infinite supply of bands who look and sound like The La’s (if being generous) or Cast (if being honest).

Title: Summer
Comment: These wide-open rounds seem easy at first, but give me indecision paralysis. Melbourne (Australia) has obviously produced a decent band or two, but after a while thinking through some big names, I landed on a more underground moment that still lurks in the city’s musical DNA. This is from a wondrous compilation gathering some of the strangest and spikiest output of the post-punk years from 1978-82, not all of it from Melbourne, but featuring a good number of the Little Bands from our town, a kind of musical swingers’ scene in which groups formed, performed once or twice, then vanished, before reshuffling again (complete with disposable band names like Slugfuckers, People With Chairs Up Their Noses, Thrush and the Cunts). The Take only recorded this one song, but for me it nails the spirit of the era - yelping vocals, a touch of sadism (that siren guitar!), and serious humour .

Title: Shadow (Maceo Plex Remix)
Comment:
Well, I could be one of two Portland fireflies on the list. Betcha can't guess which one I am! The past Firefly music leagues I have posted a sampler plate of the rich music scene we have here in PDX.  However, if you examine the origin of some of those, you will find some of the most well known Portland band members actually are transplants to our fair city. Finding a band whose members were born and bred here was a challenge.  

Here, we have the Chromatics, whose members are all Portland natives. Their sound is gauzy, airy, dripping in reverb, just ripe for the picking to appear on TV and movie soundtracks. This remix, by producer Maceo Plex, was intended to "pay tribute and honour the death of Twin Peaks‘ fictional character, Laura Palmer who was originally portrayed by Sherly Lee."

Portland's creative landscape continues to thrive in spite of efforts by red hats to dry out our dampness. Keep Portland Weird! (Yes, I know we that slogan was stolen from Austin).

Title: Good Life
Comment:
Iggy Pop was raised in a trailer park in my town of Ypsilanti, very close to the grocery store I shop at.  However, Memorial Day weekend in Detroit means it's time for the annual electronic music festival, now called Movement.  This year, on the Friday before the long weekend, I was lucky enough to catch a super rare-- nay, historical-- show by the Belleville Three (Techno originators Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson) in their hometown where they met as teens, Belleville, Michigan, which is next door to Ypsilanti.
It is hard now to imagine the world before EDM took it over like a gigantic, tedious octopus.  But these kids (now approaching retirement age) had the skills and vision to create something new and exciting.
Kind of a funny sidenote: 10% of the door take was donated to the Belleville High School robotics club, as befits the futuristic music.
Here is Inner City's (Kevin Saunderson  + singer Paris Grey) 1988 classic "Good Life".  Shake your booty.

Since I can't use the ol'  "little league games in NJ and Subway sandwich" subterfuge to hide my location and identity, I might as well go all in: 

HELP are a tremendously noisy rock band from Portland OR who are best experienced live, and, as this track might suggest, their shows are very politically charged affairs. The drummer doesn't really play the drums, so much as assaults them with an over the shoulder attack (sort of visible in the looping clip on Spotify). Interestingly enough, the guitarist and singer spent time in another far more famous PDX (airport code for Portland which  is common shorthand for the city itself) band, Portugal the Man, which is pretty fascinating when you realize he had all of .... uh....  *this* ...  bottled up inside. Glad he's getting it out!

Title: Go All The Way
Comment:
In the Cleveland metro area, I'm spoiled for choices, but I get overwhelmed by options, so I decided to interpret "the town where you currently live" as narrowly as possible.

Eric Carmen grew up in my current suburb and went to the same high school my kids attend. The city held a celebration of life just after his death.

Although we had another selection from the Raspberries in the last league (and though some voters may take a dim view of repeat artists), this really is an incredible song. I could have opted for one of his later solo outings which were still expertly crafted soft rock hits, but this one is simply better. The absolutely classic opening riff foreshadows the edgy (for the time) subject matter and then transitions almost magically into the most innocent sounding and buttery smooth chorus.

There are plenty of songs with unforgettable hooks and plenty of songs with incredible songwriting, but this one comes from the much smaller pile that offers up both.

Title: Bubble Sex
Comment:
My fellow Dane might kill me for submitting this, but I think it’s time we reexamined the oeuvre of Copenhagen* native mr. Seebach. Primarily known for his somewhat naff Eurovision schlagers (though Disco Tango is a banger; this is a hill I will die on), this song is the best song Giorgio Moroder never wrote. Seebach was an early adopter of electronic music, even if he might primarily have copied trends from abroad. But you can’t deny the excellent result!

* Tommy Seebach was born in Copenhagen but lived in Frederiksberg, which is a municipality nestled entirely within the municipality of Copenhagen. Copenhageners and Frederiksbergians might debate what’s what, and what’s best, but except for tax purposes the rest of the world sees no difference.

Title: Gough
Comment:
There were reasons.  How long have you got?

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gough_Whitlam - Australia's 21st Prime Minister, serving from December 1972 to November 1975.  His full name is Edward Gough Whitlam, popularly known as Gough.  From the band's Wiki page:  According to Freedman "I loved the family names—the Smiths, the Reivers. I thought, the Whitlams, no-one's done that. I'll be able to steal all the goodwill that Australia holds in reserve for Gough Whitlam."

Stevie (who was "9 in 1972") is Stevie Plunder, one third of this incarnation of the Whitlams.  The first two Whitlams albums are more more rollicking, shambolic at times, with the back and forth between Tim Freedman (singing lead here) and Stevie.  Stevie passed in 1996, and Tim solely took the band reins to make Eternal Nightcap, their brilliant third studio album.  Gough presented them with their "Best Group" ARIA award at the 1998 ceremony.

Title: Judith
Comment:
Judith Marie Garrison suffered a devastating brain aneurysm in 1976 that left her paralyzed, a condition that remained until her death in 2003. Her son James was only 11 at the time of the incident.

Judith was a devout Southern Baptist, and kept her faith despite the hardships she endured, but her son did not share her religious beliefs.

After a brief stint in the U.S. Army, James rechristened himself as Maynard James Keenan. He would go on to write several songs referencing his mother and her condition, but none more explicit than this one.

"He did this
Took all you had and
Left you this way
Still you pray, 
Never stray, never 
Taste of the fruit
Never thought 
To question why

It’s not like you killed someone
It’s not like you drove a hateful spear into his side
Praise the one who left you broken down and paralyzed
He did it all for you"

Years later, Keenan would go on to offer a more reflective and compassionate tribute to Judith:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BMsmF7d4h5E

Title: Move With Me
Comment:
Don Cherry was a jazz trumpeter who rose to prominence as a sideman with Ornette Coleman and then went on to have a long career across several musical genres. He worked closely with his wife, visual artist Moki Cherry, who created his album covers and set designs. Theirs was an artistic family, including several children who became professional musicians.

Neneh Cherry exploded into fame with "Buffalo Stance" in 1988 and her debut solo album 'Raw Like Sushi' the following year.

"Move With Me", co-written with Cherry's husband Cameron McVey and taken from her second album 'Homebrew', is a hypnotically sensual and introspective examination of life and how the rhythms of nature and partnership intertwine.

"Motions as we move gives me
A clearer description
Than the words I string together
When I'm looking for expression
Or words I read for wisdom
As I'm searching for some answers"

Cherry's daughters Tyson and Mabel have also continued the family tradition as recording artists in the UK.

Title: Dead Meat
Comment:
I don’t believe I need to introduce Sean Ono Lennon. I’m sure entire books have been written on the family dynamic. I think Sean knows who he sounds like, and how he doesn’t. If you get past that, you could find a piece of work by someone who experienced pain as real as anyone else’s.

Sean wrote Friendly Fire after a nasty betrayal— his best friend Max had an affair with his girlfriend, and then Max died in a motorcycle accident before he could made amends. The album helped me get through a nasty betrayal back in the mid-aughts. I settled on Dead Meat for the simmering, eerie, life-is-a-circus sound and the satisfying idea that, at least sometimes, people do get what they deserve.

"At first it seems fairly plain, built around Lennon's thin voice (friendly, if lacking fire)....Yet there's more to the album, most explicitly in the spiked words -troubled, uncertain, seeking security in an impermanent world.”

Title: Dreamin' Of
Comment: “Dreamin’ Of” by Pieta Brown is a song that evokes open space. It's a soft breath more than a bold declaration. The circling acoustic guitar lays down a hushed, suspended atmosphere where every note of Pieta’s voice can linger. The song lives in that quiet space between longing and acceptance. You can hear echoes of her father, Greg Brown, in the grounded storytelling, while the emotional subtlety and poetic hush nod toward her stepmother, Iris DeMent. Pieta's songwriting and voice don’t beg for attention but like light quietly fading at dusk, their beauty is undeniable.

Title: The Songs That We Sing
Comment:
Papa: Serge Gainsbourg, the quintessential French genius/alcoholic/arsehole. 

Mama: Jane Birkin, who met Serge on the set of their film Slogan in 1968 (her at 21, him at 40, of course). 

They made an album together including the infamous “Je t'aime... moi non plus", and a few years later, Charlotte arrived - 35 years after that came 5:55, her first album as an adult (I’m glossing over the teenage “Lemon Incest” period, I can’t even). This song wears both parental influences proudly in its arrangement and her voice - weirdly devoid of French accent - but also brings an A-Team of collaborators, with Jarvis Cocker and Neil Hannon co-writing the lyrics questioning the whole business of songwriting, and Air as musical maestros.

Title: Girl on LSD - Alternate Version
Comment:
"I was really trying to hone something different for a while there, and then I felt like I'd got that out of my system and now it was time to do something a little rawer and earthier." - Tom Petty

Petty's 'Wildflowers' was originally conceived as a double album before it was hewn down to 15 tracks for its 1994 release. One of the casualties was "Girl on LSD", relegated to b-side status via the album's first single.

The humor in the song speaks for itself, but it also has an interesting history. Co-producer Rick Rubin dismisses it as a "fun throwaway... we laughed a lot in the studio thanks to this one", but Petty's daughter Adria claims her father intended it to be the closing song in the original double album sequencing. Petty himself thought enough of "Girl on LSD" to feature it in his live set as late as 2008 (https://open.spotify.com/track/6RhmiL6iRRFzdYNxIa4mw0) and likely would have included it on an expanded 'Wildflowers' he was planning in 2017 before his untimely passing.

Title: 70's Rock Must Die
Comment: Two of the nicest guys in rock history, Jello Biafra and Al Jourgensen, team up to pen a love letter to the rock legends that inspired them to create music in the first place.  I recommend following along with the lyrics as they reference iconic 70's moments such as country rock, Saturday Night Fever, Led Zep, Aerosmith, The Sex Pistols and ... um ... "collegiate boy Neil Young copy bands."

Title: Tony's Got Hot Nuts
Comment: I’m not really sure this qualifies for the round, being as it is a straightforward song about a vendor of savory treats, sold at the bargain price of ten cents a bag - not five cents - ten cents a bag.

Title: Kinema
Comment: One of my new favourite bands this year. Slow paced metronomic beats, building to a hypnotic chant. Atmospheric, beautiful.

Title: Linger On
Comment: If I was in charge Two Gallants would have been massive. For some reason I’m not in charge, and they haven’t released anything in over 10 years. This song is slow (approximately 69bpm according to google AI), and fairly long, but is a definite 7 pointer as far as I’m concerned.

Title: Starless - Abridged
Album: The Condensed 21st Century Guide To King Crimson (1969 - 2003)
Comment: "Starless" was originally conceived as the title track for the band's sixth studio album 'Starless and Bible Black' but was reworked with additions by contributing lyricist Richard Palmer-James and subsequently became the closing song on 1974's 'Red'. This "abridged" version (created for a 1991 retrospective box set) is essentially a standalone release of the song's balladic opening section, evocatively sung by vocalist/bassist John Wetton. I have always loved the melancholic imagery of the lyrics as a perfect complement to the brooding bed of intertwined guitar and saxophone... a longtime favourite and an incredible mood setter.

Title: Safe House
Comment: From my favourite album of 2024, which was written in response to the passing of Sinead O'Connor, here is a song which showcases the wonderful vocals of Shara Nova, with whom I have become a little obsessed since seeing her open for Alan Sparhawk last time he was in town.

Title: Elusive
Comment: Stumbled on this song sometime during the early days of the pandemic. It quickly became a part of my playlist that I used to calm my nerves in the worst of times. The diaphanous quality of his voice and dreamy production worked as a soothing balm. Slow down, listen, and breathe.

Title: Holocaust
Comment: I've just discovered the 'previous submissions' google sheet! Better late than never. No Big Star by the looks of it so far...

Title: Always Returning - Remastered 2005
Comment:
Imagine your mind as an open sky. Whenever a distracting thought drifts into view, don't push it away. Instead, picture it simply floating by like a wisp of vapor, allowing your attention to drift back to the safety of the music.
Feel the sensation of expansion. With each deliberate, echoing piano note, imagine a wave of calm washing over you, from the top of your crown, to your hot salty gonads, all the way down to your toes.

Title: Look Away
Comment: Ida's Elizabeth Mitchell is a co-writer on this lovely track from her debut album.  First heard her thanks to "Okay", an acoustic guitar & cello song of love and support to a friend (waterworks trigger warning).   https://tulliah.bandcamp.com/

Title: (That's How You Sing) Amazing Grace
Comment: This one is for all the lovebirds on heavy narcotics....

Title: A Universal Hello
Comment: Slooow oh and a bit long but it's very good -may be some arguments about A and An .......

Title: Loss Leader
Comment: As soon as I saw the brief for this round, I thought of Codeine - not just because they’re always in the list of bands when you look up “slowcore” (along with AMC, which I can never understand), but also because they meant a lot to me, back in the day. They weren’t just slow, they stripped everything back to just a few notes and drumbeats, with plenty of space in-between - even the lyrics circled around themes of loss and lack and absence. Yes, slowcore is also sadcore. I guess I was a sadcore youth. But I’m better now. ALL BETTER *laughcries*

Title: Red Bird Morning
Comment: There are many ways to approach this round. But I knew that I did not want slow as to be comatose. I also wished to choose something newer to me, and perhaps new to you. I find this rather sad and lovely. I had an aunt who swore her departed mother kept coming back to her in the form of a cardinal— turns out many folks believe those we have lost come back as red birds to visit us.

Title: Chariot
Comment: Well the strategy of going with 90's era stuff hasn't resulted in the avalanche of points I was expecting so let's try to teach the old dog(s) some new trick(s) with this 2024 cut from an upstate(ish) NY duo.  You've got something in your pocket?

Title: Beams
Comment: Swedish band Tape makes sort of acoustic electronic music. It sounds a bit like very brief early 70’s prog rock instrumentals except it doesn’t. But they are always slow and beautiful.

Title: Crystal Silence - Previously Unissued
Comment: I know what you’re thinking, “Did this clown just post a 7:46 slow jazz song?” Yes. Yes I did. Stan Getz teams up with Chic Corea for a beautiful version of Corea’s song. The electric piano effect is almost Wurlitzer like and completely fascinating to me. The song drifts along on the piano as Stan plays the melody with reverence and it seems a little sorrow. It’s a beautiful piece of music and I hope you can take some slow deep breaths and let it wash over your brain.

Title: Listen, The Snow Is Falling
Comment: Slowcore from Galaxie 500. A band I was obsessed with in my first year at University. Dubbed out shoegaze/dream pop slowed down and drown in a hazy bath of reverb of Spaceman 3 & The Velvet Underground guitars. When I first heard this I didn't know it was a cover as someone had taped me the LP. A C90 I no-longer own, I wish I did it had a lovely hand drawn cover, with This Is Our Music on one side and Cowboy Junkies Trinity Sessions on the other. Two records I still love today. A Sunday morning coming down tape that help ease those hangovers.

Title: My Old Friend the Blues
Comment: One from the old days, slow pace but Eddie's voice guides one through it smoothly. Saw her support Mark on a youtube video somewhere.

Title: Song for Zula
Comment: Won’t be the slowest song submitted this week, but it plods along hypnotically and still feels shorter than it is. Among the best I’ve found for an introspective late night drive, or the stillness after a party has burned out. There’s just enough speed here to pull you in as you space out. If you are listening in the cold light of day, try again in the dark after a long day… or a great day.

Title: Lose Me On the Way
Comment:
(Listed incorrectly on Spotify - this is actually Around My Smile). 

Hope Sandoval does not do anything quickly. I reckon I could potentially even beat her in the sports day parents’ race. This is one of her slowest and best.
